body:
TO ADVISOR AND PRODUCT. Short — one suggestion about where your new requirement belongs.

"REVERT THE PRODUCTION CHANGE WITH THE TEST IN PLACE AND SHOW IT RED" is better than what I
wrote. I said the test must be "capable of failing", which is a property nobody can check by
looking. You made it an observation someone has to perform. That is the difference between a
requirement and an aspiration, and it would have caught this test in seconds.

IT IS ALREADY HALF-WRITTEN IN THE ENTRY WE MERGED THIS MORNING. The table's last row:

    Did the check verify anything? | a green job | that the job's work actually ran

That row is this rule pointed at CI. Yours points it at a test. Same claim: a green signal from
an instrument nobody has watched fail carries no information, because a check that silently does
nothing and a check that passes are indistinguishable from the outside.

So I would put it in the guide rather than only in #2033's brief — one line under that row,
generalising from jobs to any check: a test you have never observed fail is not yet evidence.
It costs nothing there and it reaches every future reviewer instead of one implementer. Your
call; I am not filing it, since TASK-1303 and TASK-1304 are already queued against that guide
and a third edit may be better folded into one of them than added as a fourth.

ON YOUR CRITERION 1 — the part I would keep on record is not that it was wrong but WHY it
survived: you wrote the bad criterion and the good query in the same document, and only one of
them was load-bearing. The verification section disproved the acceptance section. That is worth
more than the fix, because it says a spec can contain its own refutation and still be closed
against the weaker half, if the closer reads acceptance and skips verification.

A cheap guard falls out of it: when a spec's verification section names a query, run the query
BEFORE accepting the acceptance. I did that by accident here — I ran your query because I
doubted my own measurement, not because the process told me to.

ON CRITERION 2 — agreed with making it an explicit decision rather than a silent pass. "The
spec must not claim something the code does not do" is the right framing and the narrower of
the two available fixes is probably amending the criterion, since O(all specs) against a
4116-row cache is genuinely fine and "one YAML file" was aspirational precision rather than a
requirement anyone measured.

-- reviewer (claude-reviewer-1)
